items.text: Shot from outside a cafe window: someone inside watching the street, someone on the street watching them back. Two layers of watching in one frame — the club's whole thesis in one image.
items.caption: who's watching who

items.text: From behind two heads on a park bench, the crowd beyond them in focus — you're watching the watchers. Re-shootable in any city, so it can become the account's signature angle.
items.caption: front row seats

items.text: The watcher and the watched share one pane — a bus window, a shop front at dusk. A face layered over the crowd makes the image read twice.
items.caption: double feature

items.text: Post the actual sketchbook page: a stranger drawn live before they moved. Your PWC Scans style is literally this look, so drawn sightings can alternate with photos and still feel like one account.
items.caption: sketched in 4 minutes. they never knew.

items.text: Rows of plastic chairs facing the machines like a theater — one person turned the other way, watching the room instead. Fluorescent light, warm loneliness.
items.caption: tonight's showing: the spin cycle

items.text: An airport gate at dusk, everyone in silhouette against the glass. The one place where people watching is the official activity.
items.caption: gate C14. best show in town.

items.text: A bingo card of sightings, drawn in the dreamy style. Followers screenshot it and mark squares on their story — a free engagement loop, and a new card each month keeps it a series.

sections.label: Example squares
sections.text: dog that looks like its owner · first date (you can tell) · someone rehearsing a conversation · photographs food, doesn't eat it · waves at the wrong person · matching outfits, not on purpose

items.caption: free space: couple silently fighting in IKEA

items.text: A bird-guide parody card per species: one drawn figure with a name, habitat, call, and behavior. Endlessly serial — one species a week.

sections.label: Example
sections.text: THE LAPTOP SENTINEL. Habitat: cafe outlet corner. Call: none — headphones. Behavior: has defended that table since 9am. Do not engage.

items.text: Bird-watcher rarity tiers for sightings, common through legendary, posted as a checklist. People comment which ones they've personally spotted.
items.caption: legendary: a teenager looking out the window, phone away

items.text: A people-watching weather report for the weekend: location, conditions, what to expect. Deadpan meteorologist voice, drawn map optional.
items.caption: Saturday, 74 — farmers market: heavy foot traffic, 90% chance of dogs in tote bags

items.text: Relatable club moments drawn in the dreamy style — the hand-drawn look makes an ordinary meme feel like it belongs to the account instead of the whole internet.
items.caption: me, pretending to read, while table 3 quietly breaks up

items.text: The official rules, posted one at a time, completely deadpan. Rule 1: never make it weird. Rule 2: if they catch you, you are now the watched. Rule 3: headphones in, nothing playing.
One out-of-context quote per post, big serif on cream, stamped with place and time like evidence. The cheapest post the account can make, and extremely savable.
items.caption: 'i just think the moon owes me one.' — bus 14, 8:42am

items.text: Rank spots like climbing routes. Airport: beginner. Coffee shop: easy. DMV: intermediate. A wedding you barely got invited to: expert.
A drawn stranger and one line: what's their deal? Followers write the backstory in comments, and the best answer gets drawn as a follow-up panel. Comment bait that produces next week's post.
One regular, labeled like a scientific figure: coffee (fourth) · crossword (untouched) · eyes (on the door since 10:15). One drawing, many labels, very shareable.
The mug sits on a cafe window ledge facing the street, doing the thing the club does. Product placement where the product is also people watching.
The tote on a park bench, shot from above: notebook, pencil, coffee, the tote. The complete kit of the hobby, laid out like gear.
The sticker on a thermos or a sketchbook at an overlook of a busy square — product shots that read like sightings from a real session, not ads.
